title: Basic Data Interpretation Sets
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Solving a full set of questions from one table, step by step

introduction.overview: A data interpretation (DI) set gives one table or chart and then asks four to five questions about it. The questions in a basic set are of a few standard kinds: read a value, find a difference, compute a percentage change, work out an average, form a ratio, or derive a new quantity such as profit from two given columns. This chapter shows how to approach a whole set efficiently: read once, extract what is common, answer the easy questions first and keep a running record of derived values.
introduction.placementRelevance: DI sets are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, and a single set can carry as many marks as four or five separate questions. A sound routine turns the set into a reliable source of marks.
introduction.realWorldContext: Company annual reports, project dashboards and performance reviews present data in exactly this form, and decisions are made from the derived figures such as profit and growth rate.

learningObjectives: Read a data set once and note its title, units and derived quantities
Derive new columns (profit, growth, share) once and reuse them
Choose between absolute change, percentage change and ratio
Solve the easiest questions first and use approximation when options allow
Check that the answers fit the data (sign, size, units)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Profit = Revenue − Expenses. Percentage profit on expenses = Profit ÷ Expenses × 100. Percentage growth = (New − Old) ÷ Old × 100. Average = Total ÷ Count.

coreDefinitions: Data set: the table or chart together with its title, units and any notes.
Derived quantity: a value computed from the given data, such as profit (revenue − expenses) or growth rate.
Absolute change: the difference between two values. Relative (percentage) change: the difference divided by the earlier value.
Share: a part as a percentage of a whole (for example expenses as a percentage of revenue).
Base: the value that a percentage or ratio is measured against.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: In a DI set, the questions are linked: the same few derived values (profit each year, total revenue, growth rate) keep reappearing. Work them out once, write them next to the table, and every later question becomes a single look-up or one-step calculation.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Treat the table as a small spreadsheet. Add a new column in your rough work for each derived quantity that is likely to be needed (here, Profit). Fill it for all rows once.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Derived column
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Questions about profit, profit growth, profit share.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Percentage change
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The earlier value is the base.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Growth of revenue, expenses or profit.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Percentage on expenses or revenue
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Read which base the question uses.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Average over years
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Sum of values ÷ number of years
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Count the years in the table.

mainNarrative: Spend the first 20 to 30 seconds on the whole set. Read the title, the units (here ₹ lakh) and any note such as "Profit = Revenue − Expenses". Then scan the questions to see which derived quantities you will need. In this set, profit appears in many questions, so computing it for every year first is a good investment.

Solve the questions in order of difficulty. Direct readings (revenue in 2022, expenses in 2023) take seconds. Differences and totals come next. Percentage and ratio questions take longer and may be left for the end if time is short.

Percentage questions need the right base. "Percentage rise in revenue from 2020 to 2022" uses 2020 as the base: 40 ÷ 80 = 50%. "Profit as a percentage of revenue" uses revenue as the base; "profit as a percentage of expenses" uses expenses. Read the wording carefully.

Averages and growth rates: the average annual revenue is the total divided by the number of years. The average yearly increase uses the number of intervals, one fewer than the number of years: (180 − 80) ÷ 4 = 25.

Check the reasonableness of every answer. A percentage change should have the same sign as the movement of the data; an average must lie between the smallest and largest values; and a ratio of two numbers close to each other should be close to 1.

deepDiveAspects.title: Compare growth rates carefully
deepDiveAspects.content: A year with a large absolute increase need not have a large percentage increase. Revenue rose by 30 in both 2023 and 2024, but the percentage increase was 25% in 2023 and 20% in 2024, because the base was larger in 2024.

deepDiveAspects.title: Using approximation
deepDiveAspects.content: If options are far apart, round values before computing. For example, 45 ÷ 135 is exactly one-third, so 33.3%. A quick fraction often gives the answer with no long division.

problemVariations.description: Ratios and percentages of a total.
Apply a growth rate to forecast.

solvedExamples.title: Derived column and percentage on expenses
solvedExamples.question: Using the revenue and expenses table, find the profit in 2021 and the profit as a percentage of expenses in that year (to one decimal place).
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Profit = Revenue − Expenses; Profit % on expenses = Profit ÷ Expenses × 100.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The question says "on expenses", so expenses is the base.

solvedExamples.title: Percentage change in revenue
solvedExamples.question: By what percentage did revenue rise between 2020 and 2022?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The old value, 80, is the base.

solvedExamples.title: Average and total
solvedExamples.question: Find the average annual revenue and the total profit over the five years.
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Average revenue = ₹126 lakh; total profit = ₹165 lakh
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The profit column derived earlier makes the total a simple addition.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Dividing the total revenue by 4 (the number of intervals).

shortcutMethods.title: Build the derived column first

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Calculate profit afresh in each question.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Write the derived column (profit) beside the table once. Every later question then needs only a look-up or one step. Use simple fractions (45/135 = 1/3) to avoid long division.

rulesForApplication: Read title, units and notes first.
Derive common quantities once and reuse them.
Percentage change: earlier value is the base; shares: whole is the base.
Average growth per year uses the number of intervals.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Working out profit in every question.
Using revenue when the question says "on expenses".
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Underline the base words in the question.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Dividing by 5 when asked for the average annual increase.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use years − 1 for growth over intervals.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Accepting a percentage above 100 for a share.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check that the answer lies in a sensible range.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Round values and compare with the options before exact calculations; the options in DI are usually spread out.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Attempt the entire set in one go, easy questions first. Switching sets costs time because you must re-read the data.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: A neat side table of derived values is the biggest time-saver in a DI set.
